II. The Hidden Tax of Fiat Currency

Most people think of taxation as something the government does openly through legislation. But fiat money enables a far more insidious form of wealth extraction: inflation.

When the Federal Reserve creates new reserves to purchase government bonds — the process euphemistically known as "quantitative easing" — it does so without labor, without production, without adding anything of real value to the economy. The newly created dollars enter circulation first through the financial system, enriching banks, hedge funds, and asset holders. By the time these dollars circulate down to wages and consumer prices, prices have already risen. The working family, the retiree on a fixed income, the saver prudently putting money aside — they are the last to receive the new money and the first to bear its consequences.

This is not a conspiracy theory. It is the Cantillon Effect, a well-documented economic phenomenon first described in the 18th century: those who receive new money first benefit at the expense of those who receive it last. The Federal Reserve system institutionalizes this transfer of wealth. Since 1913, the dollar has lost over 96% of its purchasing power. Over the same period, the price of an ounce of gold has risen from $20.67 to thousands of dollars — not because gold became scarce, but because the paper currency measuring it became abundant.

The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises described this process with characteristic clarity: "The boom must come sooner or later. That is precisely why it is a boom. It is the essential feature of credit expansion that it must lead sooner or later to a collapse of the whole system." The Fed does not prevent booms and busts. It amplifies them, then presents itself as the cure.

III. The Moral Argument: Money Should Not Be a Political Instrument

Beyond the economic failures lies a deeper, moral argument. Money is not merely an economic tool — it is a social technology. It is the medium through which human beings coordinate their labor, express their values, and build complex societies. A sound monetary system is one where the rules are clear, predictable, and apply equally to all participants. A system where a central authority can unilaterally decide to dilute the currency, bail out favored institutions, or suppress interest rates to benefit debtors at the expense of savers is not sound. It is arbitrary.

Consider the ethical framework: If a private individual counterfeited currency, they would face criminal prosecution. When the Federal Reserve engages in essentially the same activity — creating money backed by nothing and using it to purchase real assets — it is celebrated as prudent monetary policy. This double standard reveals a fundamental contradiction at the heart of the fiat system. It presupposes that the state possesses a legitimate monopoly on the creation of purchasing power, and that this power will be exercised responsibly.

History suggests otherwise. No fiat currency in history has maintained its purchasing power indefinitely. The Roman denarius, the Byzantine solidus, the Continental dollar, the Reichsmark, the Zimbabwean dollar — the graveyard of fiat currencies is long and well-populated. The U.S. dollar, as the world's reserve currency, has managed to maintain its dominance longer than most, but its decline is well underway. The question is not whether the current system will fail, but when and how chaotically.

IV. The Alternatives: Sound Money in Practice

Critics of abolishing the Federal Reserve typically ask: "But what would replace it?" The answer is straightforward, because these systems have all been tried — with considerable success.

The Classical Gold Standard (1879–1914)

The period of the classical gold standard is often dismissed by mainstream economists as an era of deflation, stagnation, and inequality. The facts tell a different story:

  • Real GDP per capita grew at a faster rate during the gold standard era than during most of the fiat money era.
  • Deflation was generally benign, driven by productivity improvements rather than monetary contraction. Prices fell, but wages and employment grew, meaning living standards rose.
  • Interest rates were more stable and, on average, lower than in subsequent decades.
  • International trade expanded dramatically, as the gold standard provided a credible, rules-based monetary framework that reduced exchange rate risk.

The gold standard was abandoned not because it failed economically, but because it constrained government spending. The First World War demanded unprecedented military expenditure, and governments found it far more convenient to print money than to raise taxes or borrow at market rates. The gold standard did not die of natural causes. It was killed — by the political class it constrained.

Free Banking Systems

The most compelling alternative to central banking is not a single commodity-backed currency but free banking — a system in which private banks are free to issue their own banknotes and compete for customers on the basis of the soundness of their practices.

Scotland (1716–1845) provides perhaps the most celebrated historical example. Scottish free banking produced a remarkably stable monetary system over nearly 130 years. Multiple competing banks issued notes backed by gold or their own reserves, and the market disciplined them: banks with poor management or excessive note issuance lost customers to more prudent competitors. There were no bank runs, no systemic crises, and no taxpayer-funded bailouts — because there was no lender of last resort to create moral hazard.

Canada (1867–1935) offers another instructive case. Unlike the United States with its notorious "unit banking" restrictions and Federal Reserve, Canada's less regulated banking system produced larger, better-diversified banks that weathered financial storms with remarkable resilience. During the Great Depression, Canada experienced no bank failures, while the United States saw thousands. The difference was not superior central planning but greater market discipline.

In a free banking system, the competitive market — not a government monopoly — would determine which monetary standards are viable. If gold-backed money proved impractical, private issuers would innovate. We have already seen this dynamic play out with stablecoins in the digital age: private entities issuing currencies pegged to real assets, competing for trust without the threat of legal tender laws. The principle is the same whether the currency is physical or digital.

V. Answering the Objections

"Without the Fed, who would act as lender of last resort?"

This objection rests on the assumption that financial crises require a centralized rescuer. But financial crises are largely caused by centralized monetary systems. In a free banking system, banks that take excessive risks bear the consequences themselves, creating powerful incentives for prudence. Moral hazard — the tendency to take risks because someone else will bear the costs — is a feature of central banking, not a bug of free banking.

Moreover, even within the current system, the Fed's role as lender of last resort has been far more effective at bailing out irresponsible banks than protecting ordinary citizens. The 2008 bailout saved the financial system's largest institutions while millions of homeowners lost their homes. A system of private responsibility would have produced a more equitable outcome.

"A gold standard would cause deflation and economic stagnation."

This objection confuses two types of deflation: the pathological deflation caused by monetary contraction and the benign deflation caused by productivity growth. Under a gold standard, deflation is generally of the latter type. When technology and innovation reduce the cost of producing goods, prices fall. This is not a crisis — it is progress. Consumers benefit from cheaper goods, and the real value of savings increases.

The fear of deflation is largely a creation of Keynesian economics, which holds that falling prices discourage consumption. But this confuses nominal and real incentives. When a laptop costs less in dollar terms but you also earn fewer dollars, the real calculus of whether to buy now or later depends on preferences, expectations, and productivity — not on nominal price trends.

"The gold supply is too limited and volatile."

The argument that gold supply is too constrained for a modern economy reflects a misunderstanding of how monetary systems work. A gold standard does not require that every transaction be settled in physical gold. It requires that the monetary system maintain a credible, redeemable link to gold — a constraint that disciplines the creation of credit. Historically, the "gold window" was almost never invoked in ordinary commerce. What mattered was the credible commitment to redemption, not the physical movement of metal.

As for supply volatility: gold mining output has been remarkably stable over long periods, growing at roughly 1–2% per year — closely matching the growth rate of a healthy economy. This is a feature, not a bug. It prevents the monetary authority from artificially inflating or contracting the money supply to serve political ends.

"The global economy is too complex for a gold standard."

Complexity is not a valid argument against sound money. If anything, the increasing complexity of the global economy makes the arbitrary and unpredictable nature of fiat monetary policy more dangerous, not less. A rules-based monetary system provides a stable foundation upon which complex economic structures can be built. A system where a committee of twelve people in a basement in Washington can decide to create trillions of dollars at a stroke is not sophisticated — it is reckless.

VI. The Path Forward

Abolishing the Federal Reserve does not require an overnight, chaotic transition. A thoughtful path might include:

  1. An immediate audit of the Federal Reserve's operations, including all transactions with foreign central banks and private institutions, so that the American public can see how their monetary system has been managed.

  2. Legislative authorization for competing currencies, repealing legal tender laws and allowing individuals and businesses to contract in gold, silver, or any privately issued medium of exchange.

  3. A phased transition to a gold reserve requirement, beginning with a modest requirement (say, 20% backing for Federal Reserve notes) and increasing over time toward full convertibility.

  4. The eventual dissolution of the Federal Reserve as competing currencies prove viable and the need for a central monetary authority diminishes.

This is not utopian thinking. It is the restoration of a system that existed — successfully — for most of American history. The Federal Reserve is not an institution that predates the Constitution or the Declaration of Independence. It is a creature of 1913, created in response to a specific crisis, and it has outlived whatever justification it once possessed.

Conclusion

The Federal Reserve is the greatest unacknowledged source of inequality, financial instability, and political corruption in the United States. It enables the government to spend beyond its means, bails out the well-connected at the expense of ordinary citizens, and steadily erodes the savings and purchasing power of the American people. Its defenders point to the absence of 19th-century-style panics, but ignore the far greater devastation wrought by the 21st-century-style booms and busts that its policies create.

The alternatives — a gold standard, free banking, competing currencies — are not theoretical abstractions. They are historical realities, tested and proven over decades and centuries. They are grounded in the simple principle that a free people should be free to choose the money they use, and that no committee of bureaucrats can improve upon the discipline of a rules-based monetary system.

The Federal Reserve was promised to be the cure. After 113 years, it is time to acknowledge that it is the disease. It is time to restore sound money to the American people — and with it, the economic liberty and financial stability that every free society requires.

"If the American people ever allow private banks to control the issue of their currency, first by inflation, then by deflation, the banks and corporations that will grow up around them will deprive the people of all property until their children wake up homeless on the continent their fathers conquered." — Attributed to Thomas Jefferson

Abstract: The Federal Reserve System, established in 1913, is the central banking system of the United States. Over the past century, it has played an essential role in managing the nation's monetary policy and financial stability. However, this essay will argue in favor of replacing the Federal Reserve and its central banking functions, along with abandoning fiat currency, in favor of a gold standard or a free banking system that allows competing private currencies. The arguments presented will be based on the principles of sound money, free-market economics, and historical evidence.

Introduction: Fiat currency, which derives its value from the issuing government's declaration, has become the norm for most modern economies. Central banks, like the Federal Reserve, act as monetary authorities, controlling the money supply, interest rates, and overall financial stability. However, a growing number of economists have questioned the wisdom and legitimacy of central banking and fiat currency, advocating instead for a gold standard or a free banking system with competing private currencies.

Argument 1: Sound Money and Inflation The gold standard, which pegs the value of a currency to the price of gold, offers a more stable and predictable monetary system. Inflation has been a constant issue under the Federal Reserve's management of the money supply, leading to a consistent erosion of purchasing power and a growing wealth gap. By contrast, a gold standard limits the amount of currency that can be issued, preventing excessive money-printing and thus, inflation.

Argument 2: Free-Market Economics and Competition The free banking system, which allows for competing private currencies, would enable the market's natural forces to determine the value of money. Competition among various currencies would ensure that those currencies most trusted and accepted by consumers would prevail over time. This contrasts with the centralized power of the Federal Reserve, which has a monopoly over the money supply, effectively removing any form of competition or market discipline.

Argument 3: Historical Evidence and Stability Historically, the Federal Reserve has failed to prevent or mitigate severe economic crises, including the Great Depression and the 2008 financial crisis. Furthermore, central banks have often been criticized for creating economic distortions, such as asset bubbles, by setting interest rates too low for too long. A gold standard or free banking system would likely provide greater stability and avoid these pitfalls, as the money supply would be less susceptible to arbitrary manipulation.

Argument 4: Political Independence and Accountability One of the Federal Reserve's most controversial aspects is its political independence, as its members are appointed and its decisions are not subject to direct democratic control. A gold standard or free banking system, by contrast, would be more accountable to market forces and individual preferences. In such a system, the value of money would be determined by consumer behavior, not the decisions of central bankers.

Conclusion: Although the Federal Reserve and the fiat currency system have become entrenched in the United States, the arguments presented in this essay suggest that a gold standard or a free banking system with competing private currencies might be a more sound and desirable alternative. A stable and predictable monetary system based on sound principles of economics, such as free-market competition and accountability to consumer preferences, should be the ultimate goal. While the transition to such a system would undoubtedly pose challenges and require careful planning, the potential benefits in terms of greater stability, reduced inflation, and increased accountability might outweigh the risks.
